rationale: The CSF samples come from four cohorts, and differences in how each cohort was handled and measured likely shift every protein's level by site. Since scoring is within site, these shifts are only noise to the classifier. This change subtracts each protein's median within each site (no labels used) before the classifier is fitted, so it learns from within-site contrasts instead of cohort offsets.

I'm adding a second, small model built on known CSF Alzheimer's markers and averaging it with the existing full-proteome model. The markers come from Bader 2020 and the CSF glycolysis / 14-3-3 / synaptic / glial module literature. With only about 137 samples, a ridge-penalised model over about 1,000 proteins can't reliably find these weak but consistent signals. A low-variance panel model should make the ranking more stable within each site. The two models' scores are combined after z-scoring each against its own training-set scores, so the scales match across folds and sites.

Several of the strongest CSF AD markers in the panel are low-abundance proteins, such as SMOC1, NEFL, GFAP, PDYN, VSTM2A and NPTX2. The 70% detection filter probably removes them before the panel model sees them. Their missingness depends on abundance (a protein is not quantified because there is little of it), so half-minimum imputation keeps that information. I am lowering the detection threshold for panel proteins only to 30%, which lets these markers back in while the full-proteome model stays as it is.

At the moment each sample is normalised by its median over whatever proteins happen to be quantified in it. Missingness depends on abundance, so samples with more missing low-abundance proteins get an inflated median, which shifts every protein in those samples. I'm changing the median to use only reference proteins that are quantified in at least 95% of all samples. That gives a missingness-independent loading/dilution factor, which should make protein levels more comparable within each site for both the full-proteome and panel models.

Some CSF samples are contaminated with blood during lumbar puncture, and the amount varies a lot between samples. Red-cell proteins (haemoglobins, CA1, PRDX2, catalase and others) then rise along with any protein that co-varies with them. This adds noise that is unrelated to the diagnosis and that the models can wrongly pick up. Bader et al. 2020 flagged this as a major CSF quality confounder. In `featurize` I build a label-free erythrocyte-contamination score for each sample, regress it out of every protein, and drop the contamination markers themselves, so both models see protein levels without the blood signal.

Damage to the blood–CSF barrier lets liver-made plasma proteins into CSF in amounts that vary by person. That variation shifts many proteins without saying anything about Alzheimer's, so it is a second confounder like blood contamination. I'm adding a label-free leakage score built from liver plasma proteins (albumin, apolipoproteins, fibrinogens, ITIH, fetuin and others) and regressing it out of every other protein. Immunoglobulins are excluded from the score, and the leakage markers themselves are left unchanged, so intrathecal inflammation and any real barrier differences between diagnoses stay available to the model.

AD prevalence probably differs across the four cohorts, so a classifier trained on pooled data can partly learn cohort signatures as AD signal. That helps nothing under within-site scoring and adds noise. I'm giving each training sample a weight so that both classes carry equal weight inside every site, while each site keeps its share of the total. Both models then have to learn within-site diagnostic contrasts. This is different from round 1: no features are altered, only the weights in the logistic fits.

With n=137, the panel logistic model's per-protein weights are noisy. I'm adding a third ensemble component that has almost no fitted parameters: an equal-weight mean of standardised known CSF AD markers, each multiplied by its literature direction. Up in AD: glycolysis enzymes, 14-3-3 proteins, SMOC1, SPP1, chitinases, NEFL/GFAP/MAPT, NRGN/SNAP25/GAP43. Down in AD: NPTX1/2, NPTXR, VGF, PDYN, SCG2. A marker is kept only if its direction in the training fold agrees with the literature. A fixed-direction score should rank samples more stably within each site than learned coefficients do.

Keep the method the same and widen the prior-biology panel with CSF Alzheimer's markers replicated across several studies that are currently missing. These are guanine deaminase (GDA) and the 14-3-3 eta isoform (YWHAH) from the Bader 2020 tau-correlated set, plus markers from the Emory CSF module studies (Higginbotham 2020, Johnson 2022/2023): MDK and NTN1 (matrisome); CHIT1, LCP1, CD14 and ITGAM (myeloid/microglial); and SST, CRH, NPY and CBLN4 (neuropeptides, lower in AD). The panel model has been the main source of within-site stability, so better biological coverage should help more than retuning.

Within-site AUROC is the target, and the cohorts probably differ in technical offsets and AD prevalence. I'm adding a third ensemble component that picks the 50 proteins with the largest consistent AD vs non-AD effect inside each site (Hedges' g, weighted by site size, training fold only) and fits a small L2 logistic model on them. Pooled selection can be driven by between-cohort differences, so this should give stable, transferable signal. Site is used only to compute the selection statistics, never as a predictor.

I'm adding a fourth ensemble component, a diagonal-LDA style score. It sums the top 100 standardized proteins, each weighted by its within-site Hedges' g, so it has no fitted coefficients beyond the effect sizes. With n≈137 and many correlated weak markers, independence-assumption classifiers (Dudoit/Tibshirani-style nearest shrunken centroid / DLDA) often rank better than a jointly fitted logistic model. This one also uses the site-consistent effects data-driven, unlike the literature-direction score that was discarded in round 8.

All three current components are L2 logistic models, so their errors are highly correlated. I'm adding a heavily regularised shallow gradient-boosting model as a fourth ensemble member, trained on the within-site-selected proteins plus the known-marker panel. It can capture threshold and interaction effects (for example, glycolysis/14-3-3 markers rising only alongside synaptic-marker loss) that a linear score cannot. This should add diversity without much variance at n≈137. Because boosting overfits its own training scores, its test scores are z-scored over the test samples (label-free) and not against its training scores.

The gradient-boosting model added in round 12 improved the score by 0.023, so non-linear, threshold-type structure in these proteins is complementary to the three logistic models. I'm adding a heavily averaged ExtraTrees model as a fifth member, trained on the same within-site-selected and panel proteins. Its random split thresholds and bagging give a lower-variance, differently biased non-linear score, which should add diversity to the ensemble and give tree models more weight at n≈137. Like the boosting model, its test scores are z-scored over the test samples without using labels. I haven't run this yet, so its effect on the dev score is unknown.

The two tree models produced the biggest gain so far (+0.023 and +0.002), but they split on one protein at a time. That makes it hard for them to use the strongest CSF AD signal reported in recent work: the ratio of glycolysis/14-3-3/SMOC1 proteins that rise in AD to synaptic/neurosecretory proteins that fall (NPTX2, NPTXR, VGF, SCG2, PDYN), e.g. YWHAG:NPTX2. This change gives both tree models explicit log-ratio features built from the training fold's standardisation, no labels used: each up-marker against the down-marker composite, each down-marker against the up-marker composite, and an overall up-minus-down composite.

The two tree members brought the largest gains so far (+0.023 and +0.003), so I'm adding a third, differently-biased tree learner: a CatBoost model with depth-3 oblivious (symmetric) trees, ordered boosting and strong L2, trained on the same selected, panel and ratio features. Its symmetric splits learn feature interactions in a different way from LightGBM's leaf-wise trees, and it is regularised in a way known to suit very small tabular samples (n≈110 per training fold), so it should add a low-variance member whose errors overlap less with the others. Like the other tree models, its test scores are z-scored over the test samples. I haven't run this, so its effect on the dev score is unknown.

The shallow LightGBM member gave the largest single gain (+0.023), but at n≈110 per training fold its row subsampling (0.8) and column subsampling (0.5) make one seeded fit quite noisy. This change averages the raw scores of 5 LightGBM fits that differ only in random seed. The model stays the same; only seed-to-seed variance in that member's test ranking drops. I haven't run it, so the effect on the dev score is unknown.

The two tree members gave the largest gains because they added diversity in how the models are biased, not more of the same linear fit. I'm adding a sixth member: an RBF-kernel SVM on the same within-site-selected, panel and up/down-ratio features, standardised on the training fold. It makes smooth, distance-based decisions across many correlated weak markers, which neither the linear nor the axis-aligned tree models can represent, so its errors should overlap less with the others. To keep variance low at n≈110, it uses moderate C=0.5 and `gamma='scale'`, and its test scores are z-scored over the test samples without labels, as for the trees. I haven't run this, so its effect on the dev score is unknown.

The within-site selection currently ranks proteins by a size-weighted mean Hedges' g. That rule cannot tell a protein with a consistent effect in all four cohorts from one driven by a single cohort. I'm replacing the ranking with a DerSimonian–Laird random-effects meta-analytic z (pooled g divided by its standard error, which grows with between-site spread). The top 50 proteins fed to the selected-protein logistic model and both tree models should then be ones whose diagnostic effect replicates across cohorts and is stable at n≈110 per training fold. This is untested, so its effect on the dev score is unknown.

I'm adding label-free co-expression module scores as extra features for both tree members. Proteins are grouped by average-linkage hierarchical clustering on their correlation (1−r distance) in the training fold only, each module's score is the mean z-score of its proteins, and only modules with at least 5 proteins are kept. CSF AD signal is organised in co-regulated modules (glycolysis/14-3-3, synaptic, myeloid, matrisome, plasma leakage; Higginbotham/Johnson), and module averages are less noisy at n≈110 than single proteins. That gives the axis-aligned tree splits stable, pathway-level variables, building on the gain the hand-picked ratio features gave. This hasn't been run, so its effect on the dev score is unknown.

The up/down log-ratios from literature markers gave the tree models a gain in round 14. This change adds a data-driven version for the two tree models. Inside each training fold, it takes the 10 proteins with the most positive and the 10 with the most negative within-site Hedges' g. It then builds log-ratio features from them: each up-protein minus the down-composite, the up-composite minus each down-protein, and the overall up-minus-down composite. These capture cohort-specific "rise vs fall" contrasts that the fixed literature lists miss and that single-feature tree splits cannot form.
